extracted.intended_audience: comedy fans, performers, and readers interested in the history and quality of comedy roasts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging or producing comedy roast performances, contrasting historical Friars Club roasts with modern televised (Comedy Central) roasts and highlighting what makes a roast 'work' or fail. Includes examples and anti‑patterns from specific roasts and performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roasting in honor or respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts were originally 'done in honor or respect — real respect not the contemporary feigned type.' The best roasts retain an element of respect for the roastee: 'we roast the ones we love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer roasts that read as affectionate teasing rather than pure belittlement; historical Friars Club roasts and Dean Martin-era events are cited as examples where respect and celebration underlay the insults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roastee willingness to accept criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The core concept: 'funny folks airing their grievances and being willing to put up with the criticism is sound.' A roast relies on the roastee's acceptance of being the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful roast assumes mutual consent and a roastee prepared to take hits; if the roastee (or the audience) treats it as personal attack the event loses its intended dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camaraderie and playful tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive roasts convey 'a general sense of camaraderie, playful fun' among participants rather than hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor a warm, inside-joke vibe where insults are playful; anti-patterns include performances that feel mean-spirited or hostile to the point of alienating the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate guest selection / insiders vs. randoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Guests should have a sensible relationship to the roastee; the post criticizes the CC roasts for an 'odd assortment of people' including random B-list celebs that distract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate roasters who know or can serve the tone—too many unrelated or antagonistic guests (e.g., Ann Coulter at Rob Lowe roast) can derail the show and shift focus from humor to spectacle or conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous cruelty and career-harming jabs
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern roasts can veer into vindictive territory — paraphrased Hannibal Buress: 'I don’t like you... I sincerely hope this hurts your career.' This is presented as a problematic shift toward malice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of jokes framed as wishing real harm on the roastee or that aim to destroy careers; such cruelty undermines the roast's tradition of affectionate ribbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely on cheap shock or hateful slurs
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show older roasts sometimes contained racial slurs (Foster Brooks), illustrating the danger of shock for its own sake. The piece notes parallels between past and present shocking lines but flags the harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality roasts use craft and timing rather than slurs or gratuitous offensiveness; avoid content that punches down or reproduces racist/derogatory language as easy laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoiding predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts are described as 'comic comfort food' where predictability can become tedium: familiarity can 'breed...tedium and mild irritation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good roasts should introduce fresh angles, inventive targets, or new forms of joke rather than recycled one-liners and stock insults; novelty keeps an audience engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subversion and alternative approaches (anti-roasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some successful acts go 'outside the normal expectations' — examples include Norm MacDonald deciding to be the 'opposite of shocking' and Patrice O'Neal's 'anti-roast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider anti-roast strategies: deflating the expected shock, using gentle or meta humor, or reversing roast conventions to create surprise and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-humor and commentary on the roast form
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that mock the practice of roasting itself (e.g., Andy Samberg mocking the practice at James Franco's roast; Seth Rogen asking 'Why are we here, James?') can be highlights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-aware, meta jokes about the roast format can refresh the show and provide critical distance; use them to puncture formulaic moments or to critique excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone management: balance shock, craft, and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall quality depends on balancing crude/shocking elements with crafted comedy and respect for context (fundraising events, historical ritual, audience expectations). The post contrasts 'playful fun' Friars roasts with 'forced and crude' CC roasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone to the event's context (private Friars dinners vs televised specials), prioritize craft over gratuitous vulgarity, and be mindful of audience sensibilities and the roastee's standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/ritual context matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece emphasizes the Friars Club history (rituals, 'Monastary', fundraising, all‑male traditions) and implies that tradition and occasion shape what a roast should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing a roast, consider its institutional purpose (charity fundraiser, TV spectacle, private tribute) because expectations and acceptable material differ by context.
